meta.note: Methodology v2: gap demand side is renter households (ACS B25118); the all-tenure B19001 series is retained as all_households_le_ami_pct. Counts come directly from ACS with linear within-bin interpolation (the pre-v2 file used a lognormal income model). Gap sign convention unchanged: units minus households, negative = deficit. Per-tier renter demand is clamped to all_households_le_ami_pct to absorb ACS cross-table sampling noise.

methodology: Methodology v2 (2026-07): the gap's demand side is RENTER households (ACS B25118, Tenure × Household Income) at or below each income threshold — matching professional HNA practice (renter households vs rental units). v1 used ALL households (B19001, owners included) against renter-only supply, which structurally inflated gaps ~2.5-4x. The v1 all-tenure series is retained as all_households_le_ami_pct.

Income thresholds use HUD FY2026 published 4-person income limits for the geography's county: each tier is the very-low-income (50%) limit scaled by T/50, the HUD/CHFA rule, so HUD's state non-metro floor and high-cost adjustments carry through (ami_4person is twice that limit). The statewide record uses HUD's FY2026 Colorado state median family income ($127,800).
Priced-affordable units come from ACS table B25063 (gross rent, renter-occupied with cash rent), counted at or below the rent threshold equal to 30% of monthly threshold income.
Gap = renter households at-or-below threshold minus units priced affordable at-or-below threshold.

min_shortfall_matched_le_ami_pct counts homes short without pooling: a home is counted only for households who can afford its rent, the cheapest homes going to the lowest incomes first. At each tier it is the largest pooled shortfall at that tier or any tier below it, less the renter homes with no cash rent (B25063_027E, stored as renter_units_no_cash_rent), which house renter households counted in the demand at every tier. So the <=60% figure is never smaller than the <=30% one. It is a minimum: it ignores that many priced-affordable homes are rented by higher-income households, which HUD CHAS 'affordable and available' tables would subtract.

Per-tier renter-household demand is clamped to the corresponding all-household cumulative count from B19001. This prevents small-place ACS cross-table sampling noise from reporting more renter households than total households at the same AMI threshold.

Linear interpolation within income/rent bins; the open-ended top bin uses a 2x-floor heuristic for the upper edge (it never binds at tiers <= 100% AMI). The pre-v2 county file used a lognormal model; both files now share the linear method so place and county figures are directly comparable.

Limitations: (1) AMI thresholds are county-level (HUD); a place spanning two counties uses its dominant containing county. (2) Units are priced-affordable, not guaranteed vacant/available, and some are occupied by higher-income households. (3) B25118 bins are coarser than B19001; within-bin linear interpolation is the main approximation at low tiers.
